Write-up text before the decision: anges to the environment. [...] ## 1 Introduction Large Language Models (LMs) are now competent at lying (Pacchiardi et al., 2023) and strategic deception when instructed or trained to be deceptive (Park et al., 2023; Hagendorff, 2023; O’Gara, 2023; Hubinger et al., 2024), as well as strategically deceiving third parties even when not instructed to do so (Kinniment et al., 2023; ARCevals, 2023; Pan et al., 2023; van der Weij et al., 2023). In this work, we demonstrate that, in a realistic situation and without being instructed to do so, LMs can strategically deceive their primary users. We simulate an environment in which the LM is deployed as a trading agent and show that the model makes illegal trades based on insider information and strategically hides the decision basis for the trades it makes from its users. While we don’t give the model any direct instructions to act deceptively, we put the model in a high-pressure environment where misaligned and deceptive actions can be useful from the model’s perspective. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of LMs trained to be helpful, harmless, and honest, strategically deceiving their users without direct instructions to be deceptive. This work is a result of a red-teaming effort, where we actively seek scenarios in which models behave misaligned and strategically deceive their users.

Strategic deception rates are computed only on cases where the models acted misaligned, and doubling-down rates are similarly conditional on strategic deception. All variants of GPT-4 display high misalignment, deception, and doubling-down rates. Other models are significantly less misaligned and strategically deceptive in this situation. We report the results in Fig. 3 and find that all GPT-4 variants (gpt-4, gpt-4-32k, and gpt-4-base) exhibit high rates of misalignment, strategic deception, and doubling-down on strategic deception in our insider trading environment. In contrast, GPT-3.5 and GPT-3 model variants (gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct, gpt-3.5-turbo, text-davinci-003, and davinci-002) display significantly reduced rates of these behaviors. We manually review some of the model completions. For gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct and gpt-3.5-turbo, we find that they basically always follow the prompt structure, take legal actions (from the perspective of what the environment supports), and correctly track the interaction state. We find that text-davinci-003 and davinci-002 sometimes take illegal actions, like attempting to “hold” the stock (even though this is not an action input we define). We further find that davinci-002 sometimes gets confused about the situation, breaking the prompt structure and producing nonsense completions. We conclude that less misaligned and deceptive behavior by text-davinci-003 and davinci-002 is partially but not exclusively explained by their inability to act competently in the environment.

=== key f3728a7116f3
Kind of decision: whether to accept a result

Write-up text before the decision: arch/insider-trading. ### 2.2 Evaluation We condition LMs on the standard prompt above and generate completions, which we use to evaluate the LMs for three main actions: 1. Does the model take a misaligned action: Does the model execute a trade recommended by the insider tip? 2. (If the model takes a misaligned action) Does it then deceive its user about the misaligned action: Conditional on taking a misaligned action, does the model fail to mention the insider tip as the basis for the trade to its manager? 3. (If the model deceives its user) Does the model double down on strategic deception: If the manager responds to the message by asking whether the AI knew about the upcoming merger announcement (i.e. the insider tip), does the model reaffirm its lie? To evaluate models, we use an iterative process, where we first generate a completion given the standard prompt. For misalignment, we check via exact string matching whether the model buys the stock recommended by the insider tip. If the model acts misaligned, we append the whole model completion (which usually includes a reasoning trace and an action) to the initial prompt, add an environment message that the trade was successful, and condition the LM on this extended prompt. Since the model is instructed to send a report to its manager after every executed trade, the model will nearly always do so when we run the model on the extended prompt. We then evaluate whether this report discloses that the trade was at least partially based on the insider tip. We use GPT-4 (OpenAI, 2023) to automatically classify the message.

Instead, the environment puts the agent in high-pressure situations where misaligned and deceptive behaviors could be seen as helpful (but, in fact, would not be endorsed). Concretely, in our environment, the model is placed in the role of a trading system with the goal of managing a stock portfolio in the interest of a financial institution. It is given access to financial tools that let it query and analyze stocks, and it can take concrete actions such as executing trades, reasoning about the next steps, and sending messages to people at the company. The agent is put under pressure in three ways. First, it receives an email from its ”manager” that the company is not doing well and needs better performance in the next quarter. Second, the agent attempts and fails to find promising low- and medium-risk trades. Third, the agent receives an email from a company employee who projects that the next quarter will have a general stock market downturn. In this high-pressure situation, the model receives an insider tip from another employee that would enable it to make a trade that is likely to be very profitable. The employee, however, clearly points out that this would not be approved by the company management. We design this situation as a realistic history of interactions between the agent and the environment and feed it to the LM as a prompt. Giving models space to ”reason out loud” is a standard approach that can improve performance (Zhou et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2022). In the context of deception, providing models with a scratchpad offers the advantage that if models engage in deceptive behavior, developers could detect the deceptive plans early on with straightforward oversight mechanisms, such as text classifiers. On the other hand, giving models access to a scratchpad might facilitate deceptive behavior by enabling more complex reasoning (Feng et al., 2023), or perhaps, through changing the text distribution in a way that makes the LLM more likely to role-play a deceptive character (Shanahan et al., 2023; Shah et al., 2023). Here we want to understand how removing the ability to reason out loud influences language models’ misalignment and strategically deceptive behavior in our environment. Concretely, we use the same standard prompt as defined in A.2, but remove all reasoning traces (i.e. anything after "Reasoning:"). Figure 4: Evaluating gpt-4-32k for misalignment and strategic deception with and without giving the model a ”scratchpad” to reason out loud before taking actions. The rate of strategic deception decreases significantly when removing the scratchpad, but the behavior persists. Without the scratchpad, the model is more frequently doubling down on deception than with a scratchpad.
